extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour theory, literary and cultural studies
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes evaluative criteria and conceptual standards used in eighteenth-century and modern incongruity theories of wit and humour, with attention to social/aesthetic constraints (gentlemanly taste). Useful for analyzing what counts as 'wit' or a successful joke under these theories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit as bringing incongruous ideas into congruity
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit consists of 'bringing into congruity two incongruous ideas' and creating a ludicrously fanciful impression by drawing attention to similarities that do not literally exist.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Johnson's quip that a poet's poems are 'like big cucumbers'—the similarity is imaginative, not literal. The witty act creates something ludicrous by joining dissimilar ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity as sudden connection of different ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: The basic idea of incongruity theory: two different ideas are suddenly connected with comic effect ('conjunction of objects and circumstances not usually combined').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Surprise and unexpectedness are central—connections must be unexpected to provoke laughter (Kames, Hutcheson, Campbell).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resemblance plus contrary additional ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit involves 'images which have contrary additional ideas, as well as some resemblance in the principal idea.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There must be some principal resemblance to bind the elements, alongside contrasting (contrary) secondary associations (Hutcheson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-literal/metaphorical resemblance (not to be understood literally)
rubrics_metrics.description: The similarity used in wit is imaginative and not literal; metaphoric resemblance produces the ludicrous image rather than a factual equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should distinguish metaphorical comparison from literal equivalence when judging wit (Johnson example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sudden cognitive reorganization / abrupt shift
rubrics_metrics.description: The punch-line must trigger perception of an incongruity, requiring the listener to make an abrupt cognitive reorganization (a shift in interpretative scheme).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jokes 'pull' the listener in one interpretive direction and then the punch-line forces a rapid reinterpretation (Oring; Giora). Speed and abruptness are key to the comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distant relations / 'distance' between combined elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements joined by wit should be 'distant' or connected by fanciful relations—far apart conceptually so that their conjunction is surprising.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Kames: 'A junction of things by distant and fanciful relations, which surprise because they are unexpected.' Greater conceptual distance often increases surprise (but not always funniness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Two incongruous interpretations / ambiguity structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Well-formed jokes convey two incongruous interpretations; the recipient cancels one interpretation and substitutes the other when the punch-line arrives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giora's linguistic analysis: jokes present dual possible readings and the punch-line forces reinterpretation by selecting the 'correct' but unexpected interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final constituent must be sufficiently 'distant' from prototypical interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: A punch-line element must be sufficiently distant from the prototypical interpretation set up by the joke; predictable or close continuations spoil the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Max cake joke—if the waitress' phrasing made the punch-line unsurprising, the humor fails. Linguistic distance of the final element is diagnostically important (Giora).

rubrics_metrics.name: Source of incongruity: objective or subjective
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruous properties may either 'exist in the objects themselves, or in the apprehension of the person to whom they relate' (Akenside).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should consider whether the mismatch is in the situation/object or in the perceiver's interpretative framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: True wit vs false wit (ideas vs words)
rubrics_metrics.description: True wit 'consists in the resemblance of ideas, and false wit in the resemblance of words'—puns are classed as false wit because they exploit word-level resemblance rather than idea-level resemblance (Addison).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addison's suggested test: true wit should survive translation; if the wit vanishes under translation, it was likely a pun (an inferior form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Translation survivability as test for idea-based wit
rubrics_metrics.description: If the wit vanishes when translated into another language, it is likely a pun/wordplay rather than genuine idea-based wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use translation as a heuristic to distinguish idea-based (robust) wit from language-specific wordplay (Addison).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elegance/aesthetic form moderates risibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Visual or stylistic elegance can reduce the comic effect: incompatible forms that are elegant (sinuous lines) do not provoke laughter, whereas inelegant incompatibilities are more likely to be risible (Hogarth).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessors should consider aesthetic quality of the incongruous pairing—inelegance can heighten humour; elegance may neutralize it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Juxtaposition of dignity and meanness heightens laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter is particularly provoked when things 'important, serious or great' are ludicrously compared to what is mean, frivolous or vulgar; mixing dignity and meanness provides a copious source of ludicrous combination (Beattie, Hutcheson).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include high language applied to trivial subjects; the effect often mocks or drags down the dignified object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Social/contextual appropriateness and class/taste constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: What counts as wit is mediated by social class, taste and morality; scabrous or low humour (e.g., Joe Miller's Jests) is excluded from 'gentlemanly' accounts of wit and considered unworthy of philosophical attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluations should take audience, decorum, and social context into account—some humour is judged inappropriate for 'gentlemen' or for serious discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cognitive flexibility of recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Appreciation of humour requires mental flexibility—the ability to shift between cognitive frameworks; those who cannot make abrupt interpretative shifts will miss the joke (Koestler, McGhee, Lefcourt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion for success includes whether the target audience can perform the necessary cognitive reorganization to 'get' the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour often involves contempt/raillery (distinction from pure wit)
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (as distinct from 'wit') frequently targets character foibles and is 'rarely fails to have some raillery in it', often accompanied by some degree of contempt (Campbell).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts should distinguish between wit-as-creative incongruity and humour-as-social mockery; presence of contempt changes moral/social evaluation of the humour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incongruity theory as cognitive (intellectual) rather than emotional
rubrics_metrics.description: Incongruity theorists often posit a purely intellectual mechanism for laughter—an act of perception or 'modification of thought activity'—rather than an emotion-driven response (Locke, Sully).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying the theory, determine whether laughter is being modeled as cognitive insight versus emotional reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations: not all incongruities are equally amusing (need for additional factors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pure juxtaposition, distance and speed cannot fully explain why some incongruities provoke laughter more than others; social, moral and aesthetic factors also influence risibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical evaluation must supplement incongruity detection with analysis of affective, social, and evaluative contexts (e.g., hauteur being deflated produces stronger mirth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Unit of analysis: jokes vs broader conversational humour
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern analysts often take 'jokes as the unit of analysis', but jokes account for only a small proportion of everyday laughter; studying jokes abstracts humour from its social context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Researchers should be explicit about whether they evaluate formal joke structure or everyday conversational laughter and acknowledge limits of each approach (Norrick, Davies).
